title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Starting point
AI system and date: ChatGPT, 3 November 2026
Before using AI for the required extension, briefly state your question, course-based core model, baseline result, and the specific limitation or opportunity you wanted to address.
Our question is what factors most contriubte to higher daily average author revenue. Our base model is a basic linear regression model, as shown below: \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{author\_revenue}_i
={}& \beta_0
+ \sum_{j \ne j_0} \beta^{(\text{genre})}_j
  \mathbb{1}(\text{genre}_i = j) \\
&+ \sum_{k \ne k_0} \beta^{(\text{publisher})}_k
  \mathbb{1}(\text{publisher\_type}_i = k) \\
&+ \beta_1 \text{average\_rating}_i
+ \beta_2 \text{total\_reviews}_i
+ \beta_3 \text{sale\_price}_i \\
&+ \sum_{\ell \ne \ell_0} \beta^{(\text{seller})}_\ell
  \mathbb{1}(\text{seller}_i = \ell)
+ \beta_4 \text{gross\_sales}_i
+ \epsilon_i.
\end{aligned}
\]
Our main result so far is higher average ratings tend to be associated with higher revenue, and when looking at daily average gross sales, we see a pattern in publisher type—author revenue tends to increase more for indie publishers as opposed to Amazon and big five publishers. However, our dataset could have some selection bias, as the data comes primarily from bestsellers on Amazon; this makes it difficult to generalize our results.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Substantive prompts
Prompt:

I am creating a regression case study in R and Quarto. My question is what factors most contribute to higher daily average author revenue. The response is daily average author revenue, the main predictors are genre, publisher type, seller, rating, total reviews, daily average gross sales and sale price, and my course-based core model is starting_mod <- lm( author_revenue ~ genre + publisher_type + average_rating + total_reviews + sale_price + seller + gross_sales, data = publishers_data ). My main result so far is higher average ratings tend to be associated with higher revenue, and when looking at daily average gross sales, we see a pattern in publisher type—author revenue tends to increase more for indie publishers as opposed to Amazon and big five publishers. I found this limitation or opportunity: our dataset could display selection bias, as it primarily includes data from bestsellers. Suggest three feasible extensions that keep the core analysis connected to regression methods taught in my class. One option may be a meaningful model-interpretability feature applied to a model used in the case study. For each, explain how it strengthens the same research question, how its result would enter the final case study, the implementation steps, and two ways I could verify it. Do not choose for me.

Response:

A limitation to keep in view: a regression using only bestseller data can describe associations among the books in your sample, but it can’t establish that the same associations hold for all e-books. Of these options, only adding a comparable non-bestseller sample directly tests that broader question. The others assess patterns within the bestseller data.

Check whether results vary by sales-rank tier How it helps: If your data include sales_rank, compare the predictor relationships among higher- and lower-ranked books in your sample. This can show whether your conclusions depend heavily on the most prominent bestsellers.

How it could appear in the case study: Report whether the rating and gross-sales relationships look similar across rank tiers. Describe this as a robustness check within the observed bestseller sample; it does not remove selection bias.
Implementation:

Divide books into rank tiers, such as quartiles, taking care that each tier has enough observations.
Fit the core regression separately by tier, or fit one regression with rank-tier interactions for selected predictors such as average_rating and gross_sales.
Compare the estimates and uncertainty across tiers. Avoid interpreting rank as a cause of revenue.

Two ways to verify it: - Check the sample size and missingness in each tier, including whether publisher and seller categories are represented adequately.

Compare the interaction model with the model without those interactions using a partial F-test, and see whether conclusions persist under a reasonable alternative grouping of ranks.


Add a comparable sample of non-bestsellers How it helps: This lets you test whether the relationships differ between bestsellers and non-bestsellers, addressing the scope of the selection-bias concern more directly.

How it could appear in the case study: Compare the estimates for the two groups and explain whether the patterns from the bestseller sample appear to generalize. This requires non-bestseller books with comparable revenue and predictor measurements; without them, the comparison can’t be made.
Implementation:

Find a non-bestseller sample from the same platform and a comparable time period.
Confirm that author revenue, rating, reviews, price, sales, genre, publisher type, and seller are defined comparably.
Combine the samples and create a bestseller_status variable.
Fit a pooled regression with bestseller status and selected interactions, for example bestseller_status * (average_rating + gross_sales).

Two ways to verify it:

Check that the measurements, missingness, and predictor ranges are sufficiently comparable across the two groups.
Test whether the selected interaction terms jointly improve the model, then compare the estimated slopes and confidence intervals by bestseller status.


Interpret the publisher-type and gross-sales relationship with predicted slopes How it helps: Your current model is additive, so it does not directly estimate whether the gross-sales slope differs by publisher type. Adding that interaction lets you quantify and display the pattern you observed.

How it could appear in the case study: Show a plot of predicted author revenue against gross sales for each publisher type, with uncertainty intervals. Report the estimated gross-sales slope for each type. This makes the fitted associations easier to interpret, but does not correct selection bias.
Implementation:

Add gross_sales * publisher_type to the core model; this includes both main effects and their interaction.
Calculate predicted revenue over a useful range of gross sales for each publisher type, holding other predictors fixed at stated values.
Plot those predictions with confidence intervals and report the estimated slopes.

Two ways to verify it:

Compare the model with and without the interaction using a partial F-test.
Check that the plotted predictions and reported slopes agree with the fitted coefficients, and inspect whether the uncertainty intervals are wide in parts of the sales range with few books.

These are alternatives, not steps you need to combine. Whichever you consider, frame findings as associations among the sampled books unless you add data that supports broader generalization.
